title: if I knew ... / I wish I knew ...
subtitle: if I knew / I wish I knew
summary: Use if + past and wish + past to imagine a present situation that is not real, and put would in the other part of the sentence.

lesson.heading: Study this situation
lesson.text: Sarah wants to phone Paul, but she can't do this because she doesn't know his number. Sarah doesn't know Paul's number, so she says 'if I knew'. She imagines what she would do if she knew his number.

examples.text: **I'd phone** him **if I knew** his number.

lesson.heading: if + past, but the meaning is present
lesson.text: When we imagine a situation like this, we use **if + past** (if I knew / if you were / if we didn't etc.). But the meaning is present, not past.

examples.text: There are many things I'd like to do **if I had** more time.
**If I didn't want** to go to the party, I wouldn't go.
**If you were** in my position, what would you do?
It's a pity he can't drive. It would be useful **if he could**.

lesson.heading: wish + past
lesson.text: We use the past in the same way after **wish** (I wish I knew / I wish you were etc.). We use wish to say that we regret something - that something is not as we would like it to be.

examples.text: **I wish I knew** Paul's phone number.
examples.note: = I don't know it and I regret this

examples.text: Do you ever **wish you could** fly?
It's very crowded here. **I wish there weren't** so many people.
examples.note: there are a lot of people

examples.text: **I wish I didn't have** to work tomorrow, but unfortunately I do.

left.label: I'm glad (it is true)
examples: **I'm glad I live** here. (I live here and that's good)

right.label: I wish (it is not true)
examples: **I wish I lived** here. (I don't live here, unfortunately)

lesson.heading: were or was
lesson.text: After if and wish, you can use **were** instead of was (if I were / I wish it were etc.). You can also use was. Both are correct.

examples.text: **If I were** you, I wouldn't buy that coat.
I'd go for a walk **if it weren't** so cold.
examples.note: or ... if it wasn't so cold
or I wish Anna was here

lesson.heading: No would after if or wish
lesson.text: We do not usually say 'if ... would'. We use **would ('d)** in the other part of the sentence. In the same way, we do not say 'I wish ... would have' or 'I wish ... would be'.

examples.text: **If I were** rich, I would travel a lot.
Who would you ask **if you needed** help?
**I wish I had** something to read.

lesson.heading: could = would be able to / was able to
lesson.text: **Could** sometimes means 'would be able to' and sometimes 'was/were able to'.

examples.text: She **could get** a better job if she **could speak** another language.
examples.note: she could get = she would be able to get; if she could speak = if she was able to speak
I wish I could = I wish I was able

lesson.text: After if and wish, a past form talks about now: I wish I knew = I don't know now. Keep would for the other part of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Sarah doesn't know Paul's number. She says: I'd phone him if I ___ his number.
exercises.explanation: An imagined present situation: if + past (knew). We don't use would in the if-part.

exercises.prompt: ___ you if I could, but I'm afraid I can't.
exercises.explanation: The if-part has could (past), so the other part takes would: I'd help you.

exercises.prompt: We live in a city and don't need a car, but we would need one if ___ in the country.
exercises.explanation: We don't live in the country, so we imagine it with if + past: if we lived in the country.

exercises.prompt: This soup isn't very nice. It ___ better if it wasn't so salty.
exercises.explanation: The if-part has the past (wasn't), so the main part uses would: it would taste better.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with the sentence beginning I wish ...

pairs.left: I don't know many people, and I'm lonely.
pairs.right: I wish I knew more people.

pairs.left: It's cold, and I hate cold weather.
pairs.right: I wish it wasn't so cold.
I wish I was feeling better.

pairs.left: I don't know much about science.
pairs.right: I wish I knew more about science.

pairs.left: Helen isn't here, and I need to see her.

exercises.prompt: I'd make a lot of changes if ___ the manager of the company.
exercises.explanation: After if, both was and were are possible: if I was / if I were the manager.

exercises.statement: I wish I would have something to read.
exercises.explanation: I wish I had something to read. We don't say 'I wish ... would have'; use the past after wish.

exercises.prompt: I like these shoes but they're too expensive, so I'm not going to buy them. Write a sentence with if ...
exercises.answer: I'd buy them if they weren't so expensive.
exercises.explanation: Would ('d) goes in the main part; the if-part takes the past: if they weren't so expensive.

exercises.prompt: I have to get up early tomorrow, but I'd prefer to sleep late. I wish I ___ to get up early tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: Wish + past for a present situation we regret: I wish I didn't have to get up early.

exercises.statement: She could get a better job if she could speak another language.
exercises.explanation: Correct. She could get = she would be able to get; if she could speak = if she was able to speak.

exercises.prompt: We all need jobs and money, but what ___ if you didn't have to work?
exercises.explanation: The if-part is past (didn't have), so the question uses would: what would you do?

exercises.prompt: I don't want his advice, and that's why I'm not going to ask for it. Write a sentence beginning If ...
exercises.answer: If I wanted his advice, I'd ask for it.
exercises.explanation: If + past (wanted) for the imagined situation, and would ('d) in the other part.
